A rule that every column in the target table must be declared as non-null
questions.modelAnswer: A job can succeed technically while delivering wrong data, for example when an upstream export was truncated or a filter matched almost nothing. Exit codes only show that the code ran. Volume and freshness monitors are the basic observability layer: compare today's row count with a trailing average or a seasonal expectation, and alert or stop publication when it deviates beyond a tolerance. Combine this with distribution checks on key columns and schema checks, because a correct row count can still hide shifted values. Tune thresholds to avoid false alarms on legitimate swings such as weekends or holidays, and route alerts to someone who owns the dataset.

questions.stem: About 0.01 percent of records in a payments feed fail validation each day. What is the most sensible handling?
options: Repair the bad records by guessing plausible values and load them as normal
Quarantine failing records with the reason, load the valid rows, and alert if the rate rises
Fail the whole load every time that a single record turns out to be invalid
Ignore the issue completely because the percentage of bad records is so small
Silently drop the failing records, since keeping a log of them is not necessary for such a small volume
questions.modelAnswer: The right response balances completeness against safety. Quarantining keeps the pipeline flowing for the 99.99 percent of good data, while preserving the bad records with the validation error, source and timestamp so they can be investigated and replayed once fixed. Set a threshold, for example a failure rate above a few percent or any failure in a critical field, at which the pipeline stops or escalates, because a sudden jump usually means an upstream change. Failing everything for one bad record harms timeliness, silently dropping them is untraceable data loss, and guessing values invents data. In payments, reconcile quarantined amounts against control totals.

questions.stem: You rebuild a critical pipeline on new technology and must prove the new output matches the old one before cut-over. What is the most rigorous approach?
options: Run both in parallel and compare counts, key sets and column aggregates per partition
Trust the new code because it passed all of its unit tests in the CI pipeline on every commit
Compare only the total file size on disk of the old and the new output
Switch over immediately and wait for business users to report any differences
Compare only the first ten rows of each output by eye before switching over
questions.modelAnswer: Parallel running is the standard safeguard for migrations. Process identical inputs through both pipelines and reconcile at several levels: row counts per partition, sets of primary keys present in one but not the other, column-level sums, null counts and hashes of row content for exact comparison. Investigate each discrepancy, because some are real bugs and others are intended changes or floating-point and ordering differences that should be documented and agreed with business owners. Define an acceptance threshold in advance and run long enough to cover month-end or other special cases. Unit tests are necessary but do not prove equivalence on production data, and waiting for complaints is the riskiest option.

questions.stem: The data platform team receives about 200 alerts a day and has begun to ignore them, missing a real incident. What is the most effective remedy?
options: Mute the alert channel permanently, because the team already knows the platform well enough to spot real incidents
Add many more alert types so that no kind of problem can ever be missed again
Send every alert to every engineer by email so that everybody is aware
Alert on consumer-facing SLOs, route to dataset owners with runbooks, and retire the noisy alerts
Lower every alert threshold so that alerts fire earlier than they do today
questions.modelAnswer: Alert fatigue means the signal-to-noise ratio is too low. Start from what consumers care about, such as freshness by 07:00 or completeness of the revenue table, and define service-level objectives for those. Alert when an objective is at risk, not on every internal hiccup. Group related alerts into one incident, assign each dataset a clear owner, classify severity so only urgent ones page someone, and attach a runbook describing likely causes and first steps. Review alerts regularly and delete or fix those that were never actionable. More alerts or lower thresholds worsen the noise, and muting channels simply guarantees missed incidents.

questions.stem: What distinguishes ELT from the older ETL pattern?
options: ELT is a pattern used only for streaming sources, never for batch files
ELT forbids SQL transformations and requires all logic to live in application code
ELT transforms the data on a separate server before any loading into the warehouse takes place
ELT lands raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse using its scalable compute
ELT never stores the raw data, and keeps only the final transformed tables
questions.modelAnswer: In ETL, data is transformed on a separate processing server before being loaded, so only the transformed result reaches the warehouse. In ELT you land the raw data first and then transform it inside the warehouse or lakehouse, using its elastic compute and SQL. Advantages are that raw data is preserved for reprocessing, transformations can be rewritten and rerun without re-extracting from sources, and analysts and engineers can share version-controlled SQL models. Drawbacks include the need to govern raw sensitive data and to manage warehouse compute cost. ELT is not limited to streaming and does not discard raw data; keeping it is one of its main benefits.

questions.stem: In dbt, what is the main role of the ref() function when one model selects from another?
options: It deletes the referenced model after the current model has finished building
It resolves the real name of the other model and registers the dependency for build order
It downloads the referenced model from a public package registry at every run
It encrypts the referenced table so that only the current model can read it
It copies the data of the other model into the current model when the code is compiled
questions.modelAnswer: Using ref() instead of hard-coded table names does two things. First, it resolves to the correct relation for the current environment, so the same code points to a development schema while testing and a production schema in deployment. Second, it records the dependency, which lets the tool build a directed graph, run models in the right order, run only a model and its parents or children, and generate lineage documentation. Hard-coding schema and table names breaks environment isolation and hides dependencies, so the order of execution can be wrong. A similar function, source(), does the same job for raw tables outside the project.

questions.stem: An incremental model loads rows where updated_at is greater than the maximum already loaded. Some records arrive late with older timestamps and never appear. What is the best remedy?
options: Reprocess a lookback window of recent periods, with a unique key so rows merge, not duplicate
Remove the filter and always reload the complete history on every single run
Delete the records with older timestamps at the source before the model runs
Run the incremental model twice per day so that late rows get a second chance
Filter on updated_at equal to today's date only, so late rows are never loaded twice by the model
questions.modelAnswer: A strict high-water-mark filter assumes data arrives in order, which late events violate. A lookback window, for example reprocessing the last three days on every run, picks up stragglers; set it from how late data actually arrives. Because rows may be seen again, the model needs a unique key and a merge, delete-plus-insert or partition-replace strategy so reprocessing updates rows instead of duplicating them. Filtering on ingestion time instead of event time is another way to avoid missing data. Reloading the whole table is correct but costly, and is better kept for occasional full refreshes to correct drift. Running twice per day does not recover rows older than the filter.

questions.stem: An hourly job transforms a 4 TB append-only event table, and rebuilding it completely every run is too slow and costly. Which materialisation fits best?
options: A view that recomputes the whole table again every time that somebody queries it
An incremental model that processes only new data, perhaps in time-based batches
A seed file loaded from a CSV and refreshed by hand when the data changes
A full table rebuild on every run, scheduled slightly less often than hourly
An ephemeral model that is inlined into every one of its downstream consumers
questions.modelAnswer: For large append-mostly data, incremental processing does the work proportional to what changed rather than to the full history. The model selects only rows newer than what the target already holds, or processes time-sliced batches, which also supports retries and backfills of single periods. Views and ephemeral models push the cost to query time and recompute everything repeatedly. A full rebuild is simpler and always correct but wasteful at this scale. The trade-offs are complexity and drift risk: incremental logic must handle late data and deletes, so schedule occasional full refreshes or reconciliation checks to confirm that incremental and full results agree.

questions.stem: A transformation project has staging, intermediate and mart layers. What belongs in the staging layer?
options: Raw files exactly as they arrived, stored without any change whatsoever
Joins across many sources that produce wide denormalised tables for analysts
Machine learning model outputs and the features that are used to train them
Final business metrics that are ready to be used directly in dashboards and reports by executives
Light one-to-one cleaning of each source table, such as renaming and casting, with no joins
questions.modelAnswer: Staging models give every source table a clean, consistent interface: they rename columns to a convention, cast types, normalise units and timestamps, and perhaps filter out clearly invalid system rows. Keeping them one-to-one with sources and free of business logic means a source change is fixed in one place and downstream layers stay stable. Intermediate models then combine and reshape data, and marts expose business-ready entities and metrics at a declared grain. Putting joins or metrics in staging makes the logic harder to reuse and test. The raw data itself sits before staging, in the landing area, and should remain unchanged.

questions.stem: Which combination of tests best protects the declared grain of a transformation model that should have one row per order_id?
options: Uniqueness and not-null tests on order_id, plus a relationships test to the parent where relevant
A test that confirms the table name is written in lowercase letters only
No tests at all, because well-written SQL cannot produce duplicate rows
A not-null test on every column except the key, which is assumed to be correct by the source system
Only a test that confirms that the model compiles without any syntax errors
questions.modelAnswer: The grain defines which column or columns identify a row, so the most important tests assert exactly that: the key is never null and never repeated. A relationships test confirms that every foreign key points to an existing parent, catching orphans from late or missing loads. Run them on every model that others depend on, and on composite keys when the grain has more than one column. Duplicates are easy to create accidentally through a one-to-many join, which is why this check is more valuable than a compilation test. Add accepted-value and freshness tests where relevant, and make failures block deployment of downstream models when the data is critical.

questions.stem: A source system overwrites records in place and keeps no history, but analysts need the history of changes. You use scheduled snapshots to build a type 2 table. What limitation must you explain to stakeholders?
options: A snapshot table may be run only once in its lifetime, after which it is frozen
Changes between two snapshot runs are not captured, so history is only as fine as the schedule
Snapshots reproduce every single change exactly, whatever the schedule happens to be for that table
Snapshots delete the source rows once they have been copied into the history table
Snapshots work only for streaming data and cannot be scheduled like batch jobs
questions.modelAnswer: A snapshot compares the source to the previous snapshot at a given moment, then closes changed rows and inserts new versions with validity dates. If a record changes twice between runs, only the last state is seen, and a change that is reverted before the next run is invisible. The valid-from date also reflects the observation time, not necessarily when the change happened in the source. If exact history matters, use change data capture or an audit table at the source instead, or increase snapshot frequency. Be explicit that the history starts when snapshotting starts, and make sure snapshots are never full-refreshed, since the history cannot be recreated from the current state.

questions.stem: CI for a project with 1,500 models takes two hours, since every pull request builds everything. What is the best way to speed it up without reducing safety?
options: Allow merges whenever the compile step succeeds, without running any build
Run the full build only once a week and skip all checks on pull requests
Build and test only changed models and their dependants, deferring unchanged upstream to production
Remove all tests from pull requests so that the build finishes much faster
Combine all 1,500 models into one giant model that is built in a single step, which makes lineage easier to read
questions.modelAnswer: Most pull requests touch a handful of models, so slim CI selects only what changed, using state comparison against the last production run, plus everything downstream of those models. For unchanged upstream dependencies, deferral points to the existing production tables instead of rebuilding them, so the check is quick but still realistic. Keep tests on the selected models, and consider running them against a limited data sample or a clone of production for speed. Schedule a full build regularly as a backstop to catch interactions that selection might miss. Removing tests or relying on compilation only trades safety for speed, and one giant model destroys modularity and lineage.

questions.stem: What does the principle of least privilege mean for the service account that runs a data pipeline?
options: It shares the personal credentials of the engineer who originally built the pipeline
It has all permissions during the working day and none at all outside office hours
It receives administrator rights so that it never fails because of missing permissions on any resource
It receives only the permissions its tasks need, such as read on one source and write on one target
It has no permissions of its own and asks a human to approve every single action
questions.modelAnswer: Least privilege limits the damage from mistakes and compromised credentials. A pipeline that only ingests files into one landing area should be able to read its source and write to that location, and nothing else, such as deleting other buckets or reading unrelated tables. In practice, define narrowly scoped roles, grant access to specific resources, separate read and write, use different identities per environment and per pipeline, and review permissions regularly. Administrator rights are convenient but turn any bug or leaked key into a disaster, and sharing a person's credentials ruins accountability and breaks when that person leaves. A zero-permission account cannot do its work at all.

questions.stem: Why should pipelines authenticate with managed identities or IAM roles rather than long-lived access keys stored in code?
options: Roles issue short-lived credentials automatically, so there is no static secret to leak
Keys stored in code are encrypted automatically by the version control system
It is only a naming convention that has no effect on how security works
Roles make the pipeline run faster because authentication happens inside the network
Access keys cannot be used with cloud storage services under any circumstances
questions.modelAnswer: Static keys are a classic source of breaches: they get pasted into scripts, committed to repositories, copied into chat, and often never rotated. Managed identities and roles let the platform issue temporary credentials to the running workload, scoped by policy and expiring automatically, so nothing sensitive sits in code or configuration. Where a secret is unavoidable, store it in a secrets manager, inject it at runtime, rotate it on a schedule, and scan repositories for leaks. Keys in source control are not protected merely because the repository is private, since history, forks and clones spread them. The benefit is security and operational simplicity, not execution speed.

questions.stem: Which statement about encryption of data in a cloud data platform is correct?
options: Encryption at rest makes TLS unnecessary, as stored data is the only real target
Encryption in transit protects stored files from anyone who has access to the storage account or its keys
Encryption removes the need for access control, since nobody can read ciphertext
Encryption is needed only for databases, and object storage is exempt by design
Data should be protected in transit, for example with TLS, and at rest, because the threats differ
questions.modelAnswer: Encryption in transit protects data moving across networks from interception, which TLS provides between clients, services and storage. Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as disks and objects, from someone who obtains the media or bypasses normal access paths, and is typically handled with keys in a key management service, possibly customer-managed for tighter control. They guard different risks, so you want both. Neither replaces access control, because an authorised but over-privileged identity can still read plaintext through the service. Encryption also applies to object storage, backups and logs, not just databases, and key management, rotation and access to keys are part of the design.

questions.stem: Analysts need to join customer tables on email address, but must not see raw emails. Which approach best supports this?
options: Give analysts the raw emails and trust them not to misuse the information
Delete the email column and forbid analysts from joining customer tables at all
Hash the email with a public, unsalted function and document the method for analysts in the wiki
Pseudonymise the email with a keyed hash or token, and restrict access to the key or mapping
Copy the table to a shared spreadsheet from which the email column has been removed
questions.modelAnswer: A consistent pseudonym, such as an HMAC with a secret key or a token from a vault, maps the same email to the same value every time, so joins and counts work, while the original is not visible. Keep the key or token mapping in a separate, tightly controlled place, because anyone who holds it can re-identify people. Plain unsalted hashes of low-entropy values like emails can be reversed by hashing guesses, so they offer weak protection. Remember that pseudonymised data is still personal data under regimes like the GDPR and PDPA-style laws, since re-identification is possible, so access control, purpose limits and retention continue to apply. Dropping the column loses analytical value.

questions.stem: A warehouse table contains emails and phone numbers. Support staff should see full values, and analysts should see masked values. What is the best-practice mechanism?
options: Ask analysts not to select those columns and rely on their good judgement
Filter the sensitive values in the dashboard layer only, leaving the table as it is
Policy-based column masking tied to roles, with sensitive columns classified by tags
Maintain two physical copies of the table and synchronise them by hand every night
Remove the sensitive columns for everyone, including the support staff who need them
questions.modelAnswer: Enforcing the rule inside the data platform makes it consistent for every client tool. Most warehouses support dynamic masking policies or column-level grants that return the real value to authorised roles and a masked or hashed one to others. Pair that with classification tags that mark columns as personal or sensitive, so policies can be applied by tag at scale and show up in the catalogue and audits. Dashboard-only filtering is bypassable by anyone who connects with SQL or another tool, and instructions to analysts are not controls. Duplicate tables drift out of sync and multiply the surface that needs protection. Test policies with each role and log access.

questions.stem: A person asks for their personal data to be erased. Your lake stores immutable Parquet files with a table format that supports row-level deletes. What is a sound approach?
options: Find the records, delete them through the table format, then expire old snapshots and handle copies
Tell the person that data stored in a lake can never be removed once written
Rename the underlying file so that nobody is able to find the data again
Hide the row in the dashboard layer so that it is no longer visible to any user, which satisfies the erasure request
Wait for time travel to expire by itself and take no action in the meantime
questions.modelAnswer: Erasure requires deletion in every place the data lives, within the legal timeframe, so you need to know where it is: maintain a data inventory and a subject-to-key index. In table formats a DELETE or MERGE marks rows as removed, but earlier snapshots still reference old files, so follow with compaction and snapshot expiry or VACUUM to remove the files physically. Include derived tables, extracts, search indexes and backups, whose handling may follow documented retention cycles, and keep an auditable record of the request without storing the erased data. Hiding data in a dashboard is not deletion. Design for this early, for example by separating personal identifiers into small tables that are easy to purge. Confirm exact obligations with the privacy officer or legal counsel.

questions.stem: Raw web logs with full IP addresses are kept indefinitely 'in case they are useful'. From a data-protection perspective, what is the best response?
options: Hash the name of the table so that nobody is able to find the logs again
Copy them to a personal laptop for safekeeping in case the platform ever fails
Define a purpose and retention period, minimise fields, and enforce deletion with lifecycle rules
Delete all of them immediately without first checking any retention requirements or the audit obligations
Keep them forever because storage is cheap and the data might be useful some day
questions.modelAnswer: Data-protection principles such as purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation, which appear in the GDPR and in comparable laws such as Singapore's PDPA, mean you should not keep personal data longer than needed for a defined purpose. Agree with the owners and legal advisers what the logs are used for, then reduce what you store, for example by truncating or hashing IP addresses where full values are unnecessary, set retention such as ninety days for raw logs, and automate deletion with storage lifecycle policies and table retention settings so it does not depend on memory. Deleting everything at once may breach security or audit retention requirements, so decisions need documented rules, not guesswork.

questions.stem: A shared analytics platform serves several customers, and each must only see its own rows. Which control is strongest?
options: Giving all tenants one shared role and separating them by their passwords alone at the login screen
A reminder in the onboarding guide that people must only view their own rows
A filter applied by the BI tool, which users are trusted not to remove or edit
Naming conventions that put the customer name into every table and column
Row-level policies in the platform, bound to the verified tenant identity and proved by tests
questions.modelAnswer: Isolation must be enforced where the data lives, so every access path, including direct SQL, notebooks and APIs, passes through the same rule. Row-access policies or secure views evaluate the caller's identity claim, such as tenant id from the identity provider, instead of any value the user can set. For stronger separation, use separate schemas, projects or accounts per tenant at the cost of operational overhead. Prove it with automated tests that attempt cross-tenant reads and with periodic access reviews, and log all queries. BI-layer filters can be bypassed, naming conventions do nothing, and shared roles defeat the point. The choice depends on risk and scale, but enforcement belongs in the data layer.

questions.stem: A regulator asks who accessed a table of sensitive customer data in the last 90 days. What capability must have been in place?
options: A dashboard showing the row counts of each table over the past three months, with the growth rate of each
Central, tamper-resistant audit logging of data access, retained long enough and searchable
The ability to restore the table from the backup that was taken last night
A list of the engineers who created the table and who own its pipeline
Verbal confirmation from the team leads that nobody looked at the table
questions.modelAnswer: You can only answer such a question if access events were recorded before it was asked. Enable platform audit logs and query history for reads on sensitive data, send them to a central, write-protected store separate from the people being audited, retain them for the required period, and make them searchable by user, table, and time. Classification tags or a catalogue tell you which tables are sensitive, so you can scope the report quickly and set alerts for unusual access, such as bulk exports. Backups, row counts and creator lists say nothing about reads. Also consider service accounts, since automated jobs account for much access and need individual identities to be attributable.

questions.stem: Why is SELECT * discouraged when querying a large table in a columnar cloud warehouse?
options: It converts every column to text, which makes the later joins much slower
It locks the table so that no other users can query it until the scan is done
SELECT * is a syntax error in modern SQL dialects and is rejected by most engines and cloud warehouses
The engine must read every column, so more data is scanned, raising runtime and often cost
It forces the rows to be returned in a random order that changes between runs
questions.modelAnswer: Columnar storage lets the engine read only the columns a query needs. Selecting everything defeats that benefit, so wide tables with dozens of columns, some holding large text or JSON, are scanned in full. On platforms that bill by bytes scanned, that translates directly into money, and on others into longer runtimes and more compute use. List the columns you actually need, and filter early so partitions and files can be pruned. A star select is not invalid, and it is fine for a quick exploratory look with a LIMIT, though even then limits may not reduce the bytes scanned on some engines, so check the platform's rules. In views and pipelines, explicit columns also make schema changes safer.

questions.stem: What is predicate pushdown, and why does it improve performance?
options: The query text is pushed to a remote server which executes it on behalf of the client
Filters are applied as close to the data as possible, so less data is read and moved
The data is sorted before it is filtered so that later steps can run in order
Predicates are converted into stored procedures that the database runs nightly
The filtered rows are copied permanently into a cache table for later reuse
questions.modelAnswer: With pushdown, the engine hands filter conditions to the storage layer or file reader. For columnar formats such as Parquet, the reader checks min and max statistics per row group and skips groups that cannot satisfy the condition, and with partitioned data it skips entire directories. The result is much less data read from storage, fewer rows shuffled and lower cost. It works best with simple comparisons on raw columns; wrapping a column in a function, such as applying a cast or a date function to it, can prevent pushdown and cause full scans. Writing sargable conditions, and checking the query plan to confirm that filters appear in the scan, are practical habits.

questions.stem: In PostgreSQL, a query SELECT * FROM events WHERE customer_id = 42 performs a sequential scan over 500 million rows, although it returns about 200. What is the most appropriate step?
options: Disable the query optimiser so that it can no longer choose sequential scans
Add a B-tree index on customer_id and confirm with EXPLAIN that the plan uses it
Add more RAM to the database server and leave the query and the schema unchanged
Partition the table by a randomly generated column so that the rows are spread out
Replace the query with SELECT COUNT(*) so that fewer columns have to be returned
questions.modelAnswer: A highly selective filter on an unindexed column forces the database to read the whole table. An index on customer_id lets it jump straight to the matching rows, turning a scan of hundreds of millions of rows into a lookup. Use EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after to prove the plan changed and the time dropped. The trade-offs are index storage and slower inserts and updates, so index columns that queries actually use, and avoid indexing everything. Index choice also depends on data type and query patterns, such as a composite index when filters combine columns. More memory only makes the scan faster, not unnecessary.

questions.stem: A development warehouse is nearly idle, yet the bill shows it running around the clock. Which change brings the biggest saving with the least risk?
options: Enable auto-suspend with a short idle timeout and auto-resume, and add budgets or resource monitors
Increase the warehouse size so that its queries finish sooner and it sleeps more often between the bursts
Disable query logging so that fewer background operations keep the compute awake
Delete the development environment entirely and let developers share production
Switch every user to the production warehouse so that only one cluster exists
questions.modelAnswer: Compute is typically billed while it is running, whether or not queries are executing. Auto-suspend stops the compute after a short idle time, such as a minute or a few minutes, and auto-resume starts it when the next query arrives, so you pay for use rather than for availability. Add budgets, alerts or resource monitors to catch runaways, and right-size warehouses by workload instead of using one large size for all. Be aware that suspending drops local caches and a very short timeout may add cold-start delay for latency-sensitive dashboards, so tune it per workload. Enlarging the warehouse raises the hourly cost, and moving users to production only mixes workloads.

questions.stem: You need to choose clustering or sort columns for a very large warehouse table. Which guidance is most sound?
options: Cluster on every column of the table so that all possible queries are covered
Choose columns at random so that the data is spread evenly across all files
Pick columns common in filters or joins with enough distinct values, and avoid tiny tables
Choose the column that has only two distinct values to keep the key very small and the maintenance cheap
Cluster a table of a few thousand rows, because small tables gain the most
questions.modelAnswer: Clustering or sorting co-locates similar values so that the engine can skip files or micro-partitions that cannot match a filter. It pays off when queries repeatedly filter or join on a few columns, the table is large, and cardinality is enough for effective pruning, though extremely high-cardinality columns can be costly to maintain. Limit the key to a few columns, order them from most to least selective for your workload, and measure scanned bytes or partitions before and after. Maintenance such as automatic reclustering has a cost, particularly on tables with constant updates. A tiny table gains nothing, and a column with only two values prunes at most half the data.

questions.stem: A dashboard runs the same heavy aggregation over 5 billion rows hundreds of times per day. What is an appropriate optimisation?
options: Precompute the aggregate into a summary table or materialised view refreshed on a schedule
Add more filters in the dashboard so that nobody is able to see all of the data at the same time
Buy a bigger BI licence so that the dashboards can use more concurrent sessions
Ask users to open the dashboard less often so that fewer queries are sent
Remove the aggregation and show the raw rows so that nothing needs computing
questions.modelAnswer: If many users repeat the same expensive computation, do it once. A pre-aggregated table or a materialised view, refreshed incrementally or on a schedule, serves dashboards in milliseconds and cuts compute cost dramatically. The trade-off is freshness and maintenance: the summary is only as current as its last refresh, so agree an acceptable staleness with the business and show it on the dashboard. Choose the grain of the summary to match the questions people ask, and keep it consistent with the detailed data through tests. Result caching can help for identical queries but not when filters vary. Asking users to stop using a dashboard defeats its purpose.

questions.stem: Raw files in object storage are mostly accessed in the first month and rarely afterwards, yet all are stored in the most expensive tier. What is the usual solution?
options: Compress the files with a different extension and keep them in the same tier
Delete every file that is older than one week to remove the storage cost completely
Move all data to cold storage immediately, including data that is in current use
Apply lifecycle rules that move older objects to cheaper classes, noting retrieval fees
Copy everything to a second region, because storage there is always cheaper
questions.modelAnswer: Object stores offer storage classes with lower per-gigabyte prices for infrequently accessed data, at the price of retrieval charges, minimum storage durations and sometimes slower access. A lifecycle policy automates the transition by age or prefix, and can expire data at the end of its retention period. Before applying it, analyse access patterns so that frequently used data is not penalised by retrieval fees, check that tables and engines can tolerate archival tiers, since some tiers require restoring objects before reading, and align with compliance retention. Deleting after a week may violate retention or reprocessing needs, and moving hot data to cold storage can increase total cost.

questions.stem: The monthly cloud data bill rose by 60 percent in one quarter. What is the best first step?
options: Cut every team's budget by 60 percent so that the bill returns to its old level
Shut the platform down for a week to see which users complain about the outage
Attribute spend by tag, team, workload and query to find the main drivers, then target those
Ask each engineer to guess where the extra cost comes from and fix their own area of the platform
Switch to another cloud provider immediately, because prices will be lower there
questions.modelAnswer: Optimising without data wastes effort. Use cost allocation tags, billing exports and query or job history to see which services, projects, warehouses or pipelines grew, and whether the cause is more data, more users, inefficient queries, a new always-on cluster, or a one-off backfill. Usually a few items explain most of the increase. Then fix the specific causes: right-size or auto-suspend compute, fix full scans, add partition filters, set retention, and reduce duplication. Put in place budgets, alerts and showback so teams own their spend and see changes early. Arbitrary cuts or a migration are drastic, risky, and might not address the actual cause.

questions.stem: The business needs updated figures by 08:00 every day, but a team proposes an always-on streaming cluster for a 2 TB source because streaming is modern. What is the soundest engineering response?
options: Adopt streaming anyway, because a streaming job can always be made to do batch work when it is needed
Change the requirement to one-second latency so that streaming becomes justified
Choose the simplest design meeting the stated latency, here scheduled incremental batch loads
Run the streaming job and a batch pipeline in parallel on a permanent basis
Reject every pipeline that runs more often than once a day on principle
questions.modelAnswer: Architecture should follow requirements, not fashion. A daily deadline is a batch-shaped need: an incremental scheduled job costs a fraction of an always-on cluster, is simpler to operate, test and backfill, and meets the objective with margin. Streaming adds state management, late-data logic, monitoring and continuous compute cost, which is justified when business value depends on seconds or minutes of freshness, such as fraud detection or operational alerts. Document the decision along with the trigger for revisiting it, for example if consumers need hourly data. Micro-batching can be a middle path if latency tightens. Running both permanently doubles cost and creates reconciliation problems.

questions.stem: Why should pipeline code and SQL models live in version control and be changed through reviewed pull requests rather than edited directly in a production console?
options: Version control encrypts the data that the pipeline processes while it is in transit between systems
Changes become reviewable, reproducible and reversible, with a history of who changed what and why
Production consoles do not allow SQL, so code must be stored elsewhere first
It makes the code run faster in production because the files are stored compressed
It removes the need for testing because every change is already reviewed by peers
questions.modelAnswer: Version control gives a complete history, so you can see what changed, who changed it and why, compare versions during an incident, and roll back quickly to a known good state. Pull requests add peer review, automated checks and a place to discuss design, which catches many defects before they reach production. Editing in a console leaves no trace, cannot be reproduced in another environment, and makes it hard to restore what was working. Small, focused commits and descriptive messages make reviews and reverts easier. None of this speeds up execution or replaces testing; it is about traceability, collaboration and safe change, and it is the base for CI/CD and infrastructure as code.

questions.stem: You must process a 30 GB CSV file on a laptop with 16 GB of memory using Python. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Split the file by deleting every second row so that it fits into memory
Open the file in a text editor and copy the rows across to a new file by hand one piece at a time
Convert the file to an image first, since images are always smaller than text
Stream the file in chunks, or use a lazy engine, and write the results out incrementally
Read the whole file into a single in-memory list and process it all at once
questions.modelAnswer: When data exceeds memory, process it incrementally. Read the file in chunks, for example using a chunked reader or a generator that yields rows or batches, transform each chunk, and write the output as you go, keeping only small state such as running counts in memory. Alternatively use a tool designed for larger-than-memory or lazy execution, or an embedded analytical engine that can query the file directly, and consider converting the CSV once to Parquet, which is much smaller and faster to query. Loading everything into one object fails with a memory error, and discarding rows loses data. Also specify column types explicitly to avoid memory-hungry defaults.

questions.stem: What makes a data transformation function easy to unit test?
options: It is a pure function of its inputs that returns a result, with I/O kept apart from the logic
It reads directly from production databases and writes straight into dashboards without any staging
It prints its results to the console instead of returning them to the caller
It is written as one very long script that relies on many global variables
It depends on the current clock time and on random values at each call
questions.modelAnswer: A unit test needs to supply small inputs and check outputs quickly and repeatably. Functions that take data in, return data out, and avoid hidden dependencies such as the clock, global state, network calls or files can be tested with a few hand-made rows covering normal cases, edge cases like nulls and duplicates, and known bad input. Keep input and output code thin and separate, then test the logic in memory and cover the wiring with a few integration tests. Passing the date or configuration as an argument removes time dependence. Code that talks directly to production systems or relies on global variables is hard to test and risky to run.

questions.stem: Which deployment practice best fits a data pipeline team that wants safe, repeatable releases?
options: Production is changed first, and the tests are run afterwards to confirm it
CI/CD that tests, then promotes one versioned artefact through dev, staging and production
Every engineer deploys straight from a personal laptop to the production system whenever they are ready
Engineers copy the changed files to production by hand whenever they feel ready
All testing is performed in production, where the real data and users are
questions.modelAnswer: Automated pipelines make releases consistent and auditable. On each pull request, CI runs linting, unit tests and data tests against a safe environment. After merge, the same versioned artefact, such as a container image or package, is promoted from development to staging and then to production, ideally with configuration differences kept outside the code. Deployment is done by the automation with limited, logged credentials rather than by individuals, which reduces human error and enables fast rollback to a previous version. Manual copying and laptop deployments produce environment drift and no audit trail. Testing only in production means customers find the bugs.

questions.stem: Someone changes a storage bucket policy manually in the cloud console, and the Terraform plan now reports a difference. What should the team do?
options: Make every future change manually in the console and stop maintaining the code
Delete the Terraform state file so that the plan no longer reports anything
Disable the plan step in the CI pipeline so that the warning is no longer shown
Ignore the difference permanently, because the console change already works fine in practice
Treat it as drift: sync the code or revert the change, then restrict console write access
questions.modelAnswer: Infrastructure as code works only when the code is the source of truth. A difference between the declared and actual state is drift, and it may hide an insecure or undocumented change. Investigate who changed it and why. If the change was needed, express it in the code through a reviewed pull request; if not, apply the code to restore the intended state. Then reduce the chance of recurrence by limiting console permissions, alerting on out-of-band changes, and running periodic plan checks. Deleting state or disabling plans destroys the safety net, and going manual loses repeatability. Also protect the remote state with locking and access control because it can contain sensitive values.

questions.stem: For testing a pipeline end to end, which kind of test data is the most appropriate and responsible choice?
options: Customer data that has been downloaded onto personal laptops for convenience
Synthetic or anonymised data that mimics real structure and edge cases, kept apart from production
Whatever sample rows a developer happens to remember from the previous week
A complete copy of the production personal data placed in the test environment
Empty tables, because tests need no input data to prove anything about the logic of the pipeline steps
questions.modelAnswer: Tests need realistic shapes and edge cases such as nulls, duplicates, late records, odd encodings and boundary dates, but not real people's information. Generate synthetic data, or mask and sample production data through an approved process that removes or replaces direct identifiers, and keep it in a non-production environment with its own access controls. Include a small curated fixture set for unit tests and a larger realistic set for performance and integration tests. Copying production personal data into lower environments multiplies breach and compliance risk, since those environments are usually less protected. Empty tables prove nothing, and laptops are out of the organisation's control.

questions.stem: A Python pipeline that worked for months suddenly fails after a dependency released a new minor version. How should this be prevented in future?
options: Run the pipeline on a different day of the week to avoid the new release
Delete the requirements file so that no dependency version is ever constrained
Always install the newest version of every dependency each time the pipeline starts so that it stays current
Pin versions in a lock file, use a reproducible build, and upgrade deliberately with tests in CI
Avoid every third-party library and write all of the functionality in-house
questions.modelAnswer: Unpinned dependencies mean that the same code can behave differently from one build to the next. Use a lock file that records exact versions, including transitive dependencies, and build the runtime as a container image or similarly reproducible environment so development, CI and production match. Handle upgrades on purpose: use an automated tool to propose them, run the test suite, then merge, so breakage appears in a pull request rather than at 3 a.m. in production. Installing the latest at run time makes failures unpredictable. Avoiding third-party libraries altogether is impractical for data work, and the problem is not the schedule. Also scan dependencies for known vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: You inherit a 3,000-line script that mixes extraction, transformation and loading, with hard-coded paths, and the business relies on its output. How do you improve it safely?
options: Rewrite it from scratch in a new language and replace the old script on Friday
Capture current outputs as tests first, then refactor in small steps, verifying output is unchanged
Leave it untouched forever, because it works and the business relies on it
Add comments and documentation throughout but make no change to the code itself
Delete the parts of the script that look unused, then see whether anything breaks in the next production run
questions.modelAnswer: Legacy code that makes money should be changed carefully. First freeze behaviour: run the script on representative inputs and save the outputs as golden files, then write characterisation tests that fail if results differ. Next refactor in small, reviewable steps, extracting pure transformation functions, isolating reading and writing, replacing hard-coded paths with configuration, and adding logging and error handling, rerunning the tests after each step. Once logic is testable you can add proper unit tests and improve performance or structure. A big-bang rewrite loses undocumented behaviour that stakeholders rely on, and deleting seemingly unused code is risky without evidence. Run old and new in parallel before cut-over.

questions.stem: A team must rename a heavily used table column and change a data type, while dozens of downstream consumers cannot all update at the same time. Which release strategy is safest?
options: Create a new table with a different name and hide the old one without notice
Change the data type silently so that the old queries keep running unmodified
Add the new column alongside the old, migrate consumers gradually, then remove the old one
Rename the column in production immediately and let consumers fix their own queries
Wait until every consumer team agrees on a single common release day for all changes
questions.modelAnswer: The expand and contract pattern, also called parallel change, separates the migration into compatible steps. First expand: add the new column or table alongside the old and keep both populated, possibly through a view that exposes the old shape. Then migrate consumers at their own pace, using lineage and query logs to see who still reads the old column, and communicate a deprecation date. Finally contract: remove the old structure once usage reaches zero. This avoids a coordinated big-bang release and gives a simple rollback path at each step. Breaking consumers instantly causes incidents, and silent type changes risk wrong results. Contract tests can verify compatibility throughout.
